prompt:
You're reviewing a header where a 6-line block is guarded like this:

```cpp
#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_SPELLCHECK)
#include "components/spellcheck/common/spellcheck_features.h"
// ... five more lines ...
#endif
```

What should the closing line look like?
choices: `#endif  // end of block`
`#endif  // BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_SPELLCHECK)`
`#endif` with no comment — the matching `#if` is easy to find
`#endif ENABLE_SPELLCHECK`
explain: Annotate `#endif` with the condition it closes, e.g. `#endif  // BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_SPELLCHECK)`, so readers know what's ending.

choices: Leave it unconditional: `web_contents.h` is always built
Move it inside the guard: an include should always sit next to the code that uses it
Move it inside a new `#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_WEB_CONTENTS)` guard
Replace the include with a forward declaration inside the guard
explain: Guard an include only when the header itself is GN-gated. Always-built headers like `web_contents.h` stay unconditional even if only used inside a guard, and never invent buildflag names.

choices: It breaks builds with extensions off; move the include inside the `#if`
Wrap the include in `#ifdef ENABLE_EXTENSIONS`
Add a forward declaration of `IsChromeURLOverridden` instead
Nothing — an unused include is harmless in any build configuration, so leave it
explain: When a header is gated in GN, it doesn't exist in the disabled config, so its include must sit inside the same `#if BUILDFLAG(...)` block.

prompt:
Right after the regular includes of a file you see:

```cpp
#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_REWARDS)
#include "brave/components/brave_rewards/core/buildflags/buildflags.h"
#endif

#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_REWARDS)
namespace rewards { ... }
#endif
```

This is the only guarded block in the file. What should the reviewer suggest?
choices: Convert the second guard to a runtime `base::FeatureList` check
Remove the guard around the include and keep the one around the namespace
Merge them into a single `#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_REWARDS)` block
Keep both: includes and code must always have separate guards
explain: Consecutive regions with the same `#if BUILDFLAG(...)` condition should be one guard block — allowed for an include when it's the single guarded block right after the regular includes.

prompt: A file has guarded code for two different flags, each needing its own guarded include. Which layout is correct?
choices: Rewards include + code in one block, then Ads include + code in a second block
Guarded includes grouped at the top; each code block in its own guard below
One block per flag, but put the Ads block first so its include comes earlier
A single `#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_REWARDS) && BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_ADS)` around everything
explain: Includes always come first. Merging each include into its code block would put the second include after code (e.g. after a `namespace {...}`), so keep guarded includes grouped at the top.

prompt: In which situation is it acceptable to **omit** the `#endif  // BUILDFLAG(...)` comment?
choices: A 1–2 line, unambiguous block in a file that doesn't use them
A short block nested inside another `#if` block
A 5-line block that is obvious from context
A 2-line block in a file where every other `#endif` is commented
explain: Always comment `#endif` for blocks longer than 3 lines, nested blocks, or when surrounding code already does; only short (1–2 line), unambiguous blocks may skip it.

prompt: You're introducing `enable_brave_wallet` as a build flag. What should go into the public header `brave/components/brave_wallet/browser/brave_wallet_service.h`?
choices: Add `#error` in every `.cc` that includes the header
Wrap the whole header body in `#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_WALLET)` ... `#endif`
Nothing — the GN `sources` gating already keeps the header out of other builds
`static_assert(BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_WALLET));` with the buildflags include
explain: A `static_assert(BUILDFLAG(...))` in public headers catches accidental inclusion when the feature is disabled.

prompt:
```cpp
#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_BRAVE_AI_CHAT)
#include "brave/browser/ai_chat/tools/history_tool.h"
#endif

class HistoryTool;  // used only in AI-chat code below
```

A reviewer asks to wrap `class HistoryTool;` in the same buildflag guard. Best response?
choices: Agreed — every symbol tied to the feature must be guarded, including declarations
Replace the forward declaration with an unconditional include instead
Move the forward declaration inside the guarded include block
Not needed: only includes and actual usages need guards
explain: Never require `BUILDFLAG` guards for forward declarations — they pull in no dependencies. Guard the `#include` and the actual usage.

prompt:
`brave/components/foo/foo_impl.cc` is only in `sources` inside `if (enable_foo)` in BUILD.gn. It contains:

```cpp
#include "brave/components/foo/common/buildflags/buildflags.h"

#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_FOO)
void DoFoo() { ... }
#endif
```

What should the reviewer say?
choices: Fine — double-checking the flag is a cheap safety net
Replace the `#if` with `static_assert(BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_FOO));` in this `.cc`
Drop the buildflag include and the `#if`; they're redundant
Also remove the `if (enable_foo)` gating in BUILD.gn so the guard does the work
explain: A file already gated in BUILD.gn shouldn't re-check its own enable flag — it's redundant and misleading. `static_assert` safety nets are for public headers, not implementation files.

prompt: `foo_service.cc` is only compiled when `enable_foo = true`. It includes `foo/common/buildflags/buildflags.h` solely to read `BUILDFLAG(FOO_API_ENDPOINT)`, a URL passed in from GN. Is that include OK?
choices: Only if it also wraps the usage in `#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_FOO)` to be safe
Yes — reading other GN-passed values is a valid reason
No — hardcode the URL instead since the file is already gated
No — conditionally compiled files must never include buildflag headers
explain: The no-include rule covers only re-checking the enable/disable flag that already gates the file. Including the buildflag header to read other parameters is expected.
